overview.title: Finishing the JAX train_step() and the chapter 7 summary
overview.main_topic: Returning the updated metric variables as part of the JAX training state, and the six-point summary of chapter 7.
overview.central_idea: The JAX train_step() closes by collecting each metric's updated variables into new_metrics_vars and returning (logs, state) with the new state tuple. The chapter summary recaps Keras's spectrum of workflows: three ways to build models, fit()/evaluate(), callbacks, overriding train_step(), and fully custom loops.
overview.importance: The summary is a map of everything the chapter covered and of which tool to pick for which need, guided by progressive disclosure of complexity. It is the reference point for later chapters, which mostly use the Functional API with fit().

summary:
The page opens with the final lines of the JAX `train_step()` from p.253. Inside the metric loop, `new_metrics_vars += current_vars` appends the metric's updated variables (this is also what makes `num_prev = len(new_metrics_vars)` the correct offset for the next metric). After the loop, the new `state` is assembled from `trainable_variables`, `non_trainable_variables`, `optimizer_variables` and `new_metrics_vars` (callout: *Returns the new metrics variables as part of the state*), and the method returns `logs, state`. Unlike the TensorFlow and PyTorch versions, which return only the logs dict, the JAX step must return the state because nothing was mutated in place.

The authors close the section: "That was a lot of information, but by now you know enough to use Keras to do almost anything!"

The **Summary** of chapter 7 then lists six points:

- Keras offers a **spectrum of workflows** based on *progressive disclosure of complexity*, and they all interoperate smoothly.
- Models can be built with the **`Sequential`** class, the **Functional API**, or by **subclassing `Model`**; most of the time you will use the Functional API.
- The simplest way to train and evaluate is the default **`fit()`** and **`evaluate()`**.
- **Callbacks** monitor models during `fit()` and automatically act on the model's state.
- You can fully control what `fit()` does by **overriding `train_step()`** with APIs of your backend (JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch).
- Beyond `fit()`, you can write **training loops entirely from scratch** in a backend-native way, useful for researchers implementing new training algorithms.

paragraphs.what_it_says: The loop body ends by appending the updated metric variables; then a new state tuple is built with new_metrics_vars in place of the old metrics_variables, and train_step() returns (logs, state).
paragraphs.what_it_means: This is the explicit hand-back of all updated state to fit(). In the next batch, fit() will pass this state in again, so metric totals keep accumulating across the epoch.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Without returning new_metrics_vars, metric values would be reset every batch; without the append, the slicing of the next metric's variables would be wrong.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Functional state threading: (logs, state_{t+1}) = train_step(state_t, batch_t).

terminology.meaning: The tuple (trainable, non-trainable, optimizer, metrics variables) passed into and returned by the JAX train_step().

concepts.name: Progressive disclosure of complexity
concepts.definition: Keras's design principle that offers a range of workflows from very simple to fully custom, revealing complexity only as needed.
concepts.intuition: Like a camera with auto mode and full manual mode, plus everything between.
concepts.technical: Levels: Sequential/Functional + fit(); callbacks; custom train_step(); fully custom loops; all interoperable.
concepts.significance: Lets beginners and researchers use the same framework.
concepts.example: A Functional model trained with fit() whose train_step() is overridden.
concepts.misconception: That choosing a high-control workflow means giving up the simple ones elsewhere in the project.

concepts.name: Custom train_step()
concepts.definition: Overriding Model.train_step() to control what fit() does at each batch.
concepts.intuition: Swap the engine, keep the car.
concepts.technical: In JAX returns (logs, state); in TF/PyTorch returns logs.
concepts.significance: Middle level of the workflow spectrum.
concepts.example: The JAX train_step() ending on this page.
concepts.misconception: That it requires abandoning compile(); it can use self.compute_loss and self.metrics.

concepts.name: Functional API
concepts.definition: Way to build Keras models as graphs of layers by calling layers on symbolic inputs.
concepts.intuition: Wiring blocks together on a diagram.
concepts.significance: The book's default way to build models.
concepts.example: get_custom_model() on p.252; Listing 8.1 on p.256.
concepts.misconception: That it cannot be combined with subclassed models or custom train_step().

deeper.title: Choosing a workflow
deeper.body:
A practical reading of the summary (our framing, not the book's wording):

| Need | Tool |
|---|---|
| Standard model, standard training | Functional API + `fit()` |
| Act during training (stop early, checkpoint, log) | Callbacks |
| New training algorithm but keep progress bar, callbacks, metrics | Override `train_step()` |
| Everything custom (research) | Write the loop from scratch |

Each level reuses the ones below it, which is what "interoperate smoothly" means in practice.

takeaways: The JAX train_step() returns (logs, state) with new_metrics_vars as the fourth state element.
Keras workflows follow progressive disclosure of complexity and interoperate.
Sequential, Functional, subclassing: the Functional API is the everyday choice.
fit()/evaluate() are the simplest training path; callbacks add monitoring and automatic actions.
Override train_step() for custom training logic within fit(); write a full loop for brand-new algorithms.

questions.question: What does the JAX train_step() return?
questions.explanation: The final line is return logs, state. TF/PyTorch return only logs; loss and grads are intermediate values.

questions.question: Which state component is replaced by new_metrics_vars, and why must it be replaced?
questions.answer: metrics_variables; because the metric updates were computed statelessly, only the returned variables carry the accumulated metric values.
questions.explanation: See the callout 'Returns the new metrics variables as part of the state'.

questions.question: According to the summary, which model-building approach will you use most of the time?
questions.explanation: The second bullet states it explicitly. Sequential is limited to stacks, subclassing trades features for flexibility, and custom layers are components, not a model-building approach.

questions.question: Explain 'progressive disclosure of complexity' using two workflows from the summary.
questions.answer: You can start with fit() and only when needed move to overriding train_step(), keeping the rest of your code; complexity appears only when you ask for more control.
questions.explanation: The principle frames the whole chapter (p.215).

questions.question: When does the summary suggest writing a training loop entirely from scratch?
questions.answer: When you are a researcher implementing brand-new training algorithms.

questions.question: Why must new_metrics_vars += current_vars be inside the for-loop?
questions.answer: So that each metric's updated variables are collected and num_prev gives the right offset for the next metric.
questions.explanation: Its indentation on the page places it in the loop body begun on p.253.
